# Before anything else {.center background-color="#1c1c1c"}

## You have an index card {background-color="#1c1c1c" style="color:#f0f0f0"}

Write your name on it. Keep it for the next ninety minutes.

Three times today I will show you a result and ask you to commit to an answer **before** the
reveal.

Write the answer down. Do not discuss it.

I will collect the cards at the end and hand them back to you in week sixteen.

::: {.notes}
The physical commitment is the whole mechanism. Silent internal agreement produces no
learning, because students revise their memory of what they believed the moment the answer
appears. Insist on the writing. Walk around during the first demonstration and check that
people are actually doing it; after the first reveal they will do it voluntarily.

Do not introduce yourself yet. Do not show the syllabus. Administration comes at minute 80.
:::

## A question to hold onto

> What would have to be true about the world for this number to mean what I think it means?

You will be asked this in every laboratory, in every problem set, and in the capstone
rubric.

By week sixteen you should find it impossible to look at a reported result without asking it.

::: {.notes}
Put this on the board and leave it up all semester if the room allows. It is the one-line
compression of the entire course.
:::

# Part 1 — Three ways to be confidently wrong {background-color="#1c1c1c"}

## The setup {background-color="#1c1c1c" style="color:#f0f0f0"}

Three analyses.

Each performed competently. Each using methods you already know. Each producing a
confident, well-formatted, publishable answer.

Each answer is wrong.

None of the three errors is a modelling error.

::: {.notes}
Say "none of the three is a modelling error" slowly. It is the thesis and it will not be
believed until after the third demonstration.
:::

## Demonstration one: an admissions decision

A university is investigated for discrimination in graduate admissions.

Here are the aggregate figures.

| Applicants | Admitted | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| Men | 3,738 of 8,442 | **44%** |
| Women | 1,494 of 4,321 | **35%** |

A nine-point gap across more than twelve thousand applications.

::: {.notes}
Berkeley 1973, Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell in *Science*, 1975. Do not name it yet; some
students will recognise it and that is fine, but naming it early converts the exercise from
a demonstration into a recitation.
:::

## The same data, by department

| Department | Men applied | Men admitted | Women applied | Women admitted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 825 | **62%** | 108 | **82%** |
| B | 560 | **63%** | 25 | **68%** |
| C | 325 | **37%** | 593 | **34%** |
| D | 417 | **33%** | 375 | **35%** |
| E | 191 | **28%** | 393 | **24%** |
| F | 373 | **6%** | 341 | **7%** |

Four of six departments favour women. The aggregate favours men.

## Card, question one {.center}

::: {style="font-size:1.4em"}
**Which analysis is correct — the aggregate, or the department-level one?**

Write: *aggregate*, *departments*, or *neither*.
:::

::: {.notes}
Collect the room's split verbally before revealing. Usually 70 percent say departments,
20 percent neither, 10 percent aggregate. Whatever they say, the correct answer is that the
question is malformed, which is where we go next.
:::

## The answer is: the question is malformed

Neither analysis is "correct" until you say **what you are trying to estimate**.

::: {.fragment}
**Estimand A** — the total effect of applicant gender on admission probability.
Do *not* adjust for department. Department is a mediator: women applied to more competitive
departments.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Estimand B** — the direct effect within a department, holding department fixed.
*Do* adjust.
:::

::: {.fragment}
These are different questions with different answers. Both numbers are correct. Neither is
*the* answer.
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the first appearance of the estimand-first discipline, which is Step 4 of the spine.
Do not develop the formalism now. The point is only that "which analysis is right" is not
answerable without a stated target.
:::

## Simpson's paradox is the easy version

Most of you have seen this before. Here is the version that is genuinely counterintuitive.

Adjusting for a variable can **create** an association that does not exist.

Twenty lines of code, no data required.

::: {.notes}
Everyone knows Simpson's paradox as trivia. Almost nobody has internalised collider bias,
because the verbal argument does not convince and it has to be seen numerically. This is why
we simulate.
:::

## Collider bias, simulated

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 100_000

# Two genuinely independent causes.
talent = rng.normal(size=n)
looks  = rng.normal(size=n)

print(np.corrcoef(talent, looks)[0, 1])
# -> -0.002   (independent, as constructed)

# Hollywood casts you if you have EITHER talent OR looks.
famous = (talent + looks) > 1.5

print(np.corrcoef(talent[famous], looks[famous])[0, 1])
# -> ?
```

::: {.notes}
Run this live if you can. The live run is worth more than the slide. Pause before revealing
the second number and take a show of hands on the sign.
:::

## Card, question two {.center}

::: {style="font-size:1.4em"}
**Among famous people, is talent correlated with looks?**

Write: *positive*, *negative*, or *zero*.
:::

## The result

```python
print(np.corrcoef(talent[famous], looks[famous])[0, 1])
# -> -0.63
```

A strong **negative** correlation, between two variables that are independent by
construction.

::: {.fragment}
Nothing was measured badly. The sample size is 100,000. The code is four lines.

The error is that we conditioned on a **common effect** of both variables.
:::

::: {.notes}
The magnitude surprises people. Emphasise that no amount of additional data helps, and that
a larger sample makes the wrong answer more precise.

If time permits, note that this is why "among hospitalised patients", "among survivors",
"among funded startups", and "among published studies" are all dangerous phrases.
:::

## What just happened

```
    talent ──┐
             ├──> famous     ← we conditioned here
    looks  ──┘
```

::: {.fragment}
`talent` and `looks` are independent. `famous` is a **collider** on the path between them.

Conditioning on a collider opens a path that was closed.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The folk rule "adjust for everything you have" is wrong, and this is why. Weeks 2–4 give you
the machinery to know which variables to adjust for and which to leave alone.
:::

## Demonstration one: the lesson

The analysis was competent. The arithmetic was correct. The sample was large.

::: {.fragment}
The failure happened **before any modelling**, at the point where someone decided which
variables to include.
:::

::: {.fragment}
No cross-validation would have caught it. No better model would have fixed it.
:::

## Demonstration two: a clinical risk model

A hospital asks you to predict which patients will be readmitted within thirty days.

You build a model. Here is the evaluation.

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| AUROC | **0.97** |
| Accuracy | 0.94 |
| Precision | 0.91 |
| Recall | 0.88 |
| 5-fold CV, stratified | stable across folds |

Held-out test set. Nothing was tuned on it.

::: {.notes}
Let this sit. Let someone say "that's suspiciously good" — there is usually one. Agree that
it is suspicious, and then ask them what specifically they would check. Most cannot answer,
which is the point.
:::

## Card, question three {.center}

::: {style="font-size:1.4em"}
**Would you deploy this model?**

Write: *yes*, *no*, or *what I would check first*.
:::

## The feature importances

```python
model.feature_importances_.sort_values(ascending=False).head(6)
```

```
discharge_disposition_code    0.412
number_inpatient              0.183
discharge_date                0.121
num_medications               0.077
time_in_hospital              0.064
age                           0.041
```

::: {.fragment}
`discharge_disposition_code` records **where the patient went when they left**.

One of its values means "transferred to another acute care hospital."
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the Diabetes 130-US hospitals dataset structure, which we use again in week 8. The
leak is real and is present in many published analyses of it.
:::

## Three kinds of leak, all present here

::: {.fragment}
**1. Outcome-adjacent features.** A variable recorded at or after the moment the outcome is
determined. Here: discharge disposition and discharge date.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**2. Treatment as predictor.** The clinician already suspected the risk and acted on it. The
model learns to predict *the clinician*, not the patient. It will fail the moment protocols
change.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**3. Preprocessing leak.** Imputation and scaling fitted on the full dataset before
splitting. Small, silent, and present in a large fraction of student projects.
:::

## After removing the leaks

| Metric | Leaky | Clean |
|---|---|---|
| AUROC | 0.97 | **0.68** |
| Precision | 0.91 | 0.31 |
| Recall | 0.88 | 0.44 |

::: {.fragment}
0.68 is a *reasonable* readmission model. The literature lives around there.

The 0.97 was never a model. It was a description of the label.
:::

::: {.notes}
Worth saying explicitly: the honest model is the one that looks worse. Students spend three
years being rewarded for higher numbers, and this course inverts that incentive. Say so now
and again at minute 80.
:::

## Demonstration two: the lesson

::: {.fragment}
The failure was in **evaluation design**, not in the model.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A random train-test split was the wrong split. The correct split is temporal: train on
earlier admissions, test on later ones, because that is how the model would be used.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You will measure the size of this gap at least three times this semester, in three different
domains.
:::

## Demonstration three: a trading strategy

A cross-sectional equity signal, tested on twenty years of daily data.

| | |
|---|---|
| Annualised return | 14.2% |
| Annualised volatility | 9.1% |
| **Sharpe ratio** | **1.56** |
| Max drawdown | −11.4% |
| Alpha vs. Fama-French 5-factor | 6.8% (t = 3.1) |

Out of sample. Net of a 10 basis point transaction cost assumption.

::: {.notes}
Show an equity curve if you have one; a smooth upward line does more work than the table.
:::

## Card, question four {.center}

::: {style="font-size:1.4em"}
**Would you allocate capital to this strategy?**

Write: *yes*, *no*, or *what I would ask for*.
:::

## The construction

```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

strategies = []
for i in range(200):
    # A signal built from pure noise, by construction.
    signal  = rng.normal(size=(n_days, n_stocks))
    returns = backtest(signal, prices, cost_bps=10)
    strategies.append(returns)

best = max(strategies, key=sharpe)
print(sharpe(best))
# -> 1.56
```

::: {.fragment}
The signal contains **no information**. It is noise.

You have been shown the maximum of two hundred draws, presented as if it were one.
:::

## The two hundred siblings

The reported Sharpe of 1.56 is the maximum of a distribution.

::: {.fragment}
The expected maximum Sharpe of $N$ independent worthless strategies grows roughly like
$\sqrt{2\log N}$.

For $N = 200$ over 20 years, a Sharpe near 1.5 is **exactly what you should expect from
nothing**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The t-statistic of 3.1 was computed as if one hypothesis had been tested. Two hundred were.
:::

::: {.notes}
Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) argue the effective threshold for a new factor should be a
t-statistic near 3 rather than 2, precisely because of the size of the search. Mention the
paper; it is assigned in week 9.
:::

## The uncomfortable part

You would not have done this deliberately.

::: {.fragment}
You would have tried a few signal definitions. Adjusted a lookback window. Tried a different
universe. Dropped a bad year. Re-run with a different rebalancing frequency.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Then reported the one that worked.
:::

::: {.fragment}
That is the same procedure. The only difference is that the search was informal, so you did
not count it.
:::

::: {.notes}
This lands hardest of the three, because students can see themselves doing it. It
generalises well beyond finance: the same thing happens with model specifications, feature
sets, and preprocessing choices in every domain.
:::

## Demonstration three: the lesson

::: {.fragment}
The failure was in **uncertainty quantification**. The reported interval accounted for
sampling variation and nothing else.
:::

::: {.fragment}
In most applied work, sampling variability is the *smallest* of the uncertainties.
Specification uncertainty and search uncertainty dominate, and neither appears in a standard
confidence interval.
:::

# Part 2 — The diagnosis {background-color="#1c1c1c"}

## What the three have in common {background-color="#1c1c1c" style="color:#f0f0f0"}

::: {.fragment}
None was a failure of technique.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None would have been fixed by a better model, more compute, more data, or more
cross-validation.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Each occurred at a different point in a process that most of you have never been taught
explicitly.
:::

## Where your prior training stopped

Undergraduate data science hands you:

- a clean dataset
- a well-posed question
- a metric to optimise

::: {.fragment}
Every one of today's three failures happens *outside* that boundary — in choosing the
question, constructing the data, or designing the test.
:::

::: {.fragment}
This is not a criticism of your prior courses. It is a statement about what is left.
:::

## The thesis of this course {.center}

::: {style="font-size:1.3em"}
This course is **not** about better models.

It is about the steps on either side of the model, where nearly all real errors live.
:::

::: {.notes}
Pause here. This is the hinge of the lecture. Everything before it was evidence; everything
after it is the plan.
:::

## Two courses, one problem

You are taking *Big Data Analytics* alongside this. The division is deliberate.

| | Big Data Analytics | This course |
|---|---|---|
| Central question | Can we compute it? | Does it mean what we think? |
| Failure taught | Job dies, cluster idles | Confident, well-formatted, wrong |
| Core objects | Partitions, task graphs, columnar formats | Estimands, assumptions, estimators |
| Artefact | A pipeline that scales | A claim with an error bar |

## The test

::: {style="font-size:1.15em"}
If the interesting thing about a task **disappears** when you shrink the data to a thousand
rows —

it belongs in *Big Data Analytics*.
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:1.15em"}
If the interesting thing **survives** at a thousand rows —

it belongs here.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Several datasets appear in both courses. Gaia, the taxi records, exchange tick data,
Sentinel-2. Same data, different question.
:::

# Part 3 — The methods spine {background-color="#1c1c1c"}

## Nine steps, twelve domains {background-color="#1c1c1c" style="color:#f0f0f0"}

Every project this semester runs through the same nine-step rubric.

The domain changes. The skeleton does not.

::: {.fragment}
This is the actual content of the course. Astronomy, genomics, and procurement fraud are the
delivery mechanism.
:::

::: {.notes}
Warn them that the repetition will feel excessive around week 7 and that this is intended.
The transfer happens on roughly the fifth repetition, when they start recognising which step
a new problem is really about before they know anything about the domain.
:::

## The spine

::: {style="font-size:0.9em"}
1. **Provenance** — where did these numbers come from, and who gained by producing them?
2. **Schema** — what is the shape, and what invariants must hold?
3. **Measurement** — what do the values measure, and what does absence mean?
4. **Estimand** — what number am I trying to learn, and what makes it identifiable?
5. **Estimation** — which estimator, and why that one?
6. **Uncertainty** — how wrong could this be, and from how many sources?
7. **Evaluation** — how would I know if it were wrong?
8. **Reproducibility** — can someone else get this number again?
9. **Communication** — who acts on this, and what decision improves?
:::

::: {.notes}
Hand this out on paper in week one. Students should be able to recite it by week sixteen and
should structure every report around it.
:::

## Step 1 — Provenance and acquisition

> Where did these numbers come from, who produced them, why, and what did they gain or lose
> by producing them?

Data are not found objects. Someone chose an instrument, a sampling frame, a coding scheme,
and a retention policy — usually for reasons unrelated to your analysis.

::: {.fragment}
**Five questions you will answer in writing for every project:**

1. What is the unit of observation, precisely?
2. What is the target population, and how does the sampling frame differ from it?
3. What was measured, and what was derived, imputed, or modelled upstream?
4. Has this been revised since publication, and does the archive keep the vintage you need?
5. If someone had an incentive to influence these numbers, how would they do it?
:::

## Step 2 — Schema, contracts, structure

> What is the shape of the data, what invariants must hold, and how do you detect violations
> automatically?

You already know SQL, so this step moves fast. We push past querying into modelling.

::: {.fragment}
- Dimensional modelling; entity-relationship reasoning over messy sources
- **Valid time vs. transaction time** — when something was true, versus when the database
  learned it
- Automated validation that fails a pipeline rather than warning
- Tidy long format vs. wide analysis matrix, and when to move between them
:::

::: {.notes}
The bitemporal distinction is week 11 material but plant it now. "What did we believe about
this supplier on the date the contract was awarded?" is a question a non-bitemporal warehouse
simply cannot answer.
:::

## Step 3 — Measurement and missingness

> What do the recorded values actually measure, and what does absence mean?

::: {.fragment}
A laboratory value is absent because nobody ordered the test.

Nobody ordered it because the clinician was not worried.

The clinician's worry is what you are trying to predict.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**The missingness is more informative than the value.**
:::

::: {.fragment}
MCAR / MAR / MNAR and the limits of that taxonomy · measurement error, classical and
Berkson · attenuation bias · construct validity · censoring vs. truncation · digit
preference and heaping
:::

## Step 4 — Estimand and identification

> What number am I trying to learn, defined **without reference to any estimation
> procedure**?

::: {.fragment}
You will be forbidden from writing code until you have written a sentence of this form:

> *I want to estimate the average change in $Y$ that would result from setting $X$ from
> $x_0$ to $x_1$, in population $P$, at time $t$.*
:::

::: {.fragment}
Only then does the question of method arise.

This is the demonstration-one failure, and it is the single most valuable habit this course
can give you.
:::

## Step 5 — Estimation

> Given the estimand and the identification argument, which estimator, and why that one?

::: {.fragment}
- Regression as **adjustment** versus regression as **prediction** — different objects
- A regularised coefficient is not an estimate of anything in particular
- Matching, weighting, doubly robust estimators
- The bootstrap and its failure cases
- When a simple difference in means is right and adding covariates makes things worse
:::

::: {.notes}
Note how short this slide is relative to the others. Estimation is the part students already
over-weight; the course deliberately spends less time here than they expect.
:::

## Step 6 — Uncertainty

> How wrong could this be, and from how many sources?

::: {.fragment}
You arrive with Bayesian machinery, which is an advantage. The gap is elsewhere:
:::

::: {.fragment}
In most applied work, **sampling variability is the smallest of the uncertainties**.

Specification uncertainty, measurement uncertainty, and cleaning-choice uncertainty dominate
— and none of them appear in a standard confidence interval.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Multiverse and specification-curve analysis · calibration · proper scoring rules ·
sensitivity to unmeasured confounding · multiplicity in all its disguises
:::

## Step 7 — Evaluation

> How do you know the answer is good, using a test the answer could actually fail?

::: {.fragment}
**The recurring lesson of this course:** a random train-test split is almost always the wrong
split, and the amount by which it flatters you is a measurable quantity.

You will measure it at least three times.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Splits that respect dependence — temporal, spatial, group, patient, cluster ·
negative controls · placebo tests · injection-recovery · offline-versus-online divergence
:::

## Step 8 — Reproducibility

> Can someone else — including you in six months — obtain this number again?

You know Git and Docker, so this is brisk. The parts you will not have seen:

::: {.fragment}
- Data versioning (DVC, or content-addressed snapshots with recorded checksums)
- Explicit dependency graphs (Snakemake, Make)
- Environment pinning that actually pins
- Seeding, and the reproducibility of stochastic algorithms across library versions
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Hard requirement, every deliverable:** one command regenerates every number in the report
from raw data.
:::

## Step 9 — Communication and decision

> Who acts on this, what decision are they making, and what does your output need to look
> like for that decision to improve?

::: {.fragment}
- A result is a **claim with a stated uncertainty**, not a metric
- Communicating a null result
- Statistical significance is not a decision-relevant statement
- Decision curve analysis; expected-value-of-information reasoning
- Writing for a reader who stops after the first paragraph
:::

## Mapping today back to the spine

| Demonstration | Failed at |
|---|---|
| Admissions / collider | **Step 4** — estimand and identification |
| The 0.97 AUC | **Step 7** — evaluation design |
| The 1.56 Sharpe | **Step 6** — uncertainty under search |

::: {.fragment}
Three failures, three different steps, zero modelling errors.
:::

::: {.notes}
This slide is the payoff of the first hour. Take a moment on it.
:::

## Why the same rubric, twelve times

::: {.fragment}
Because a domain tour teaches domain trivia.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Students who spend two weeks each on genomics, finance, and satellite imagery — learning a
different vocabulary in each — leave with twelve sets of facts and no transferable skill.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The rubric is what transfers. By week nine you should be able to open an unfamiliar dataset
in a domain you know nothing about and say, within twenty minutes, which step is going to
be the hard one.
:::

# Part 4 — Infrastructure {background-color="#1c1c1c"}

## Laptop-first, deliberately {background-color="#1c1c1c" style="color:#f0f0f0"}

Every project this semester runs on **16 GB of RAM, four cores, no GPU**, within a working
session.

::: {.fragment}
This is not a limitation. It is a pedagogical choice.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A course where every project begins with "spin up a cluster" teaches you to reach for
infrastructure before thinking. The other course inoculates you against that. This one must
not undo it.
:::

## The stack

::: {style="font-size:0.85em"}
| Layer | Tools |
|---|---|
| Environment | Python 3.11+, `uv` or conda, lockfile committed |
| Numerics | NumPy, pandas / Polars, SciPy, scikit-learn, statsmodels |
| Causal | `DoWhy`, `EconML`, `linearmodels`, `dagitty`, staggered-DiD packages |
| Data | **DuckDB**, Arrow, Parquet |
| Validation | Pandera or Great Expectations |
| Orchestration | Snakemake or a plain Makefile |
| Data versioning | DVC, or checksummed snapshots |
| Survival | `lifelines`, `scikit-survival` |
| Geospatial | `xarray`, `geopandas`, `rioxarray`, `h3` |
:::

Domain-specific Docker images are published per week. Pull them before the laboratory.

## Making large data fit: three techniques

::: {.fragment}
**1. Columnar formats with pushdown.** Convert to Parquet; read only the columns and row
groups you need. A 200 GB CSV frequently becomes a 4 GB Parquet file you never fully read.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**2. DuckDB over files.** Query Parquet, CSV, and remote HTTP ranges directly in SQL, with
out-of-core execution. You already know SQL, so this is free capability.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**3. Principled subsetting.** Spatial bounding boxes, time windows, seeded random or
stratified samples.

The discipline: the subset must be reproducible **from the recipe**, never shipped as a file
of unknown provenance.
:::

## DuckDB, concretely

```sql
-- No ingestion step. No server. Out-of-core.
SELECT
    pickup_zone,
    date_trunc('hour', tpep_pickup_datetime) AS hr,
    count(*)          AS trips,
    median(trip_distance) AS med_dist
FROM read_parquet('s3://nyc-tlc/yellow_tripdata_2024-*.parquet')
WHERE trip_distance BETWEEN 0.1 AND 100
GROUP BY 1, 2;
```

::: {.fragment}
This runs on your laptop against hundreds of millions of rows, because Parquet lets the
engine skip everything it does not need.

Roughly a third of the "big data" problems you will meet this semester dissolve here.
:::

## The one-command rule

Every deliverable, without exception:

```bash
$ make all
```

::: {.fragment}
regenerates **every number, table, and figure** in the report from raw inputs.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Not "the notebook runs." Not "here are the cells in order."

One command, from a clean checkout, on a machine that is not yours.
:::

::: {.notes}
Enforce this from problem set one. It is far cheaper to establish in week 5 than to retrofit
in week 15, and the capstone rubric allocates 10 percent to it.
:::

## When you may use the cluster

There is a modest HPC allocation. You must justify each request. Four legitimate reasons:

::: {.fragment}
1. **Irreducible scale** — subsetting would change the scientific question (all-sky Gaia
   clustering; multi-year Sentinel-2 over a large region).
2. **Embarrassingly parallel simulation** — the best use of a small cluster, and the
   recommended way to validate a method.
3. **The one transformer fine-tune** in week 10, which has a CPU fallback.
4. **Once, for calibration** — so you have felt the difference between eleven hours and
   eleven minutes rather than been told about it.
:::

## Ethics is graded, in context

Three themes recur, taught where they arise rather than as a bolted-on lecture:

::: {.fragment}
**Re-identification.** Data anonymous per record and identifying in combination. We run the
actual attacks — trajectory unicity, the taxi medallion hash — because attacks are memorable
and principles are not.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Harm from correct models.** A well-calibrated model can produce an unjust system.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Accusation from anomaly.** In week 11 you will produce a ranked list of suspicious
entities. At realistic base rates most of the top of that list is innocent. You will compute
and report that number *before* naming anyone.
:::

# Part 5 — The contract {background-color="#1c1c1c"}

## Accuracy is not graded {background-color="#1c1c1c" style="color:#f0f0f0"}

::: {style="font-size:1.25em"}
Model performance appears **nowhere** in the capstone rubric.
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:1.15em"}
A capstone that finds a null result, correctly, with a good design, earns full marks.
:::

::: {.notes}
Say this twice. Nobody believes it the first time, because three years of coursework have
taught the opposite. Put it in writing in the handbook and refer back to it when the first
problem set is returned.
:::

## The capstone rubric

::: {style="font-size:0.85em"}
| Criterion | Weight |
|---|---|
| Provenance and acquisition | 10% |
| Schema and validation | 10% |
| Measurement and missingness | 15% |
| **Estimand and identification** | **20%** |
| Estimation and uncertainty | 15% |
| Evaluation | 15% |
| Reproducibility | 10% |
| Communication | 5% |
:::

That is the spine, weighted. Nothing else is graded.

## Causal inference is the gate

Weeks 2–4 are an intensive block: potential outcomes, DAGs, confounding, colliders,
difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, sensitivity analysis.

::: {.fragment}
It is examined in **week 4**, separately and early, and it is worth 20 percent.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The examination format: four scenarios described in words. Draw the DAG, name the estimand,
name the identification strategy, name the threat, specify one falsification test.

**No estimation required.**
:::

::: {.fragment}
Students who can do this can learn any estimator later. Students who cannot will misuse every
estimator they learn.
:::

## Defect hunts

Every laboratory notebook contains at least one **seeded defect**.

::: {.fragment}
A leaked feature. A join that silently duplicates rows. A random split where a grouped split
is required. An imputation that destroys the signal.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You find it, name it against the spine, and fix it. This is graded at 10 percent.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The purpose is to convert passive execution into diagnosis. Assume every notebook I give you
is broken, because it is.
:::

## Assessment

| Component | Weight |
|---|---|
| Causal inference examination (week 4) | 20% |
| Four problem sets | 20% |
| Defect-hunt participation | 10% |
| **Capstone project** | **40%** |
| Peer review of one capstone | 10% |

::: {.fragment}
The peer review is graded on the quality of the criticism. You will find that the errors you
spot easily in someone else's work are the ones you made yourself.
:::

## The capstone

Choose **any project from the catalogue that we did not cover in class**.

::: {.fragment}
Twelve domains at survey depth in the taught weeks. One domain in real depth, chosen by you.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Proposal due week 9. Presentations week 16.

The catalogue document has thirty-four projects with datasets, methods, and references. Read
the chapters that interest you before week 9.
:::
